before: The museum is a federal state budgetary cultural institution, the Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War 1941 to 1945, run by the Russian state with the Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation as its parent body. Its general director is Alexander Shkolnik, who was honoured by Putin in 2021 for patriotic education and sanctioned by the UK and Australia in 2022. The museum describes itself as a centre of patriotic education for new generations and for countering falsification of history.
after: Federal museum under Russia's Ministry of Culture. Its director Alexander Shkolnik was honoured by Putin in 2021 for patriotic education and sanctioned by the UK and Australia in 2022.

before: Opened on Poklonnaya Hill on 9 May 1995 in a building by Anatoly Polyansky with 14,143 square metres of permanent galleries; the 2022 exhibition Ordinary Nazism drew 150,000 visitors in its first month.
after: Opened on Poklonnaya Hill on 9 May 1995 in Anatoly Polyansky's building; the 2022 exhibition Ordinary Nazism drew 150,000 visitors in its first month.

before: Patriot Park is the Central Military-Patriotic Park of Culture and Recreation of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, built and funded by the Russian Defence Ministry, which allocated more than 20 billion rubles to it in 2015. It covers 5,414 hectares including a 3,530 hectare military base and hosts the ministry's annual Army forum. Its head Vyacheslav Akhmedov was arrested for fraud in August 2024 together with a Defence Ministry general.
after: Built and funded by Russia's Defence Ministry, which allocated over 20 billion rubles in 2015. Its head Vyacheslav Akhmedov was arrested for fraud in August 2024 with a ministry general.

before: Conceived by Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu and opened in stages from 2015 to 2016; Putin called it a major component of the system of military-patriotic education for young people.
after: A 5,414 hectare site with a 3,530 hectare military base, hosting the ministry's Army forum; conceived by Sergei Shoigu and opened from 2015 to 2016.

before: From 2002 to 2026 the museum was run by the Foundation for Research on Central and Eastern European History and Society, a public foundation chaired by Mária Schmidt and financed by the Hungarian government, which gave it 5.5 billion forints in 2019. On 1 September 2026 the foundation was dissolved and its tasks passed to Kulturális Vagyonkezelő Kft, a company under the Ministry for Social Relations and Culture. Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr dismissed Schmidt on 15 September 2026 and ordered a content review of the exhibition.
after: Mária Schmidt's public foundation ran it from 2002 to 2026 on government money, 5.5 billion forints in 2019. Since September 2026 a culture ministry company, Kulturális Vagyonkezelő Kft, runs it.

before: Housed at Andrássy út 60, the former Arrow Cross and ÁVH headquarters; the museum drew millions of visitors over 24 years and is the Hungarian public collection most visited by foreigners.
after: At Andrássy út 60, once Arrow Cross and ÁVH headquarters. Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr dismissed Schmidt on 15 September 2026 and ordered a content review.

before: The museum is a state cultural institution supervised and financed by Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, which appoints its director. The culture minister dismissed the PiS-appointed director Grzegorz Berendt in March 2024 and appointed Rafał Wnuk, a co-author of the original exhibition. The museum merged with the Westerplatte Museum in 2017 on the order of Culture Minister Piotr Gliński.
after: A state institution financed by Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, which appoints its director. In March 2024 the minister replaced PiS appointee Grzegorz Berendt with Rafał Wnuk.

before: The museum is a public institution of the Ho Chi Minh City government, belonging to the city's Department of Culture and Sports. It is owned by the Vietnamese state and funded from the city budget and ticket income. It has received more than 25 million visitors in 50 years, about 500,000 a year, two thirds of them foreigners.
after: A public institution of the Ho Chi Minh City government under its Department of Culture and Sports, funded from the city budget and ticket income.

before: Opened 4 September 1975 at 28 Võ Văn Tần; one in six international visitors to the city tours it.
after: Opened 4 September 1975 at 28 Võ Văn Tần; about 500,000 visitors a year, two thirds of them foreigners.

before: The museum is a public service unit directly under Vietnam's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, with its functions set by ministerial Decision 2372/QD-BVHTTDL of 2025. The decision assigns it propaganda and education work on Ho Chi Minh's life, thought and revolutionary ethics, and it manages state-assigned finances and assets and collects fees. It has received more than 40 million visitors, over 10 million of them foreign.
after: A public service unit under Vietnam's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, which by Decision 2372/QD-BVHTTDL of 2025 sets its propaganda and education tasks and lets it collect fees.

before: Founded by a Party Secretariat resolution of 25 November 1970 and opened 19 May 1990 on Ho Chi Minh's centenary in a lotus-shaped building by Soviet architect Garon Isacovich; holds 130,000 documents and artefacts.
after: Founded by a 1970 Party resolution and opened 19 May 1990, Ho Chi Minh's centenary, in Garon Isacovich's lotus-shaped building; over 40 million visitors.

before: The museum is owned and operated by Kültür A.Ş., the culture company of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, which began construction in 2005 and opened it in January 2009. It is financed by the municipality through Kültür A.Ş. and by ticket sales. Posocco describes it as one of Istanbul's most popular attractions for domestic and foreign tourists.
after: Owned and run by Kültür A.Ş., the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's culture company, which built it from 2005 and opened it in January 2009. Financed by the municipality and ticket sales.

before: Built at Topkapı beside the point where the Ottomans breached the walls in 1453; opened with praise from Prime Minister Erdoğan after three years of construction.
after: Built at Topkapı where the Ottomans breached the walls in 1453; opened after three years with praise from Prime Minister Erdoğan.

before: The museum is maintained by Yasukuni Shrine, which has been a private religious corporation since 1946 after the Occupation's Shinto Directive abolished state sponsorship of Shinto. The revamped museum reopened in July 1986.
after: Maintained by Yasukuni Shrine, a private religious corporation since 1946, when the Occupation's Shinto Directive ended state sponsorship of Shinto. The revamped museum reopened in July 1986.

before: The building is owned by Roma Capitale, the City of Rome, and run by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo, a municipal instrumental body founded in 1998 that operates under an annual service contract with the city. Palaexpo also manages the Scuderie del Quirinale and Casa del Jazz and reports one of the highest self-financing rates among Italian cultural bodies. The city's Office for Education and Culture oversees it.
after: Owned by Roma Capitale and run under a city service contract by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo, a 1998 municipal body that also runs the Scuderie del Quirinale and Casa del Jazz.

before: The hall is run by the National Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall Management Office, an agency of Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, and funded from the central government budget. The Ministry of Culture directs its transformation under the government's transitional justice policy and negotiated the 2024 honour guard change with the Ministry of National Defense. The honour guard itself is provided by the military.
after: Run and funded from the central budget by an agency of Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, which directs its transformation and negotiated the 2024 honour guard change with the defence ministry.

before: Construction began 31 October 1976 and the hall opened 5 April 1980 with a 6.3 metre bronze statue of Chiang; the changing of the guard is a major tourist attraction.
after: Built from 31 October 1976 and opened 5 April 1980 with a 6.3 metre bronze statue of Chiang; the changing of the guard draws tourists.

before: The site is owned by the Venezuelan state and controlled by the Ministry of Defense and the Bolivarian National Militia, whose headquarters have been there since 2008. The government organises the visits and the Presidential Honour Guard guards the sarcophagus; the staging of the mausoleum was the responsibility of the state. Since 1981 it has had museum status as the Military History Museum.
after: State-owned, controlled by the Ministry of Defense and the Bolivarian National Militia, based there since 2008. The state organises visits and an honour guard watches the sarcophagus.

before: Built 1904 to 1906 in the 23 de Enero district; by 2014 it received about 800 visitors a day and 2,000 at weekends, and acting president Delcy Rodríguez renewed her oath at the tomb on 6 January 2026 after Maduro's capture.
after: Built 1904 to 1906 in 23 de Enero. Acting president Delcy Rodríguez renewed her oath at the tomb on 6 January 2026 after Maduro's capture.

before: The museum is a Ukrainian state museum with national status granted by presidential decree on 21 June 1996, financed from the state budget under the Ministry of Culture, which renamed it in July 2015 under the decommunisation laws and reports on its decolonisation work. Its director general is Yurii Savchuk. In 2023 the museum replaced the Soviet emblem on the Motherland Monument's shield with the Ukrainian trident.
after: A state museum financed from the state budget under the Ministry of Culture, which renamed it in July 2015 under the decommunisation laws. Its director general is Yurii Savchuk.

before: The 102 metre Motherland Monument houses the main exhibition on an 11 hectare site; more than 21 million visitors since 1981.
after: The 102 metre Motherland Monument houses the main exhibition; in 2023 the Soviet emblem on its shield gave way to the Ukrainian trident.

before: The museum is run by the Stiftung Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, a non-profit foundation under civil law funded by annual matching contributions from the Free State of Saxony and the City of Dresden, with further grants from federal bodies, businesses and foundations. Its board of trustees is chaired by Dresden mayor Annekatrin Klepsch with Saxon state minister Barbara Klepsch as deputy. Iris Edenheiser has been director since 2022.
after: Run by the Stiftung Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, a non-profit foundation funded by matching annual contributions from Saxony and the City of Dresden, with further grants from federal bodies, businesses and foundations.

before: Founded 1912 by Odol manufacturer Karl August Lingner; about 220,000 visitors in 2004.
after: Founded 1912 by Odol manufacturer Karl August Lingner. Dresden mayor Annekatrin Klepsch chairs its trustees and Iris Edenheiser has directed it since 2022.

before: The museum is the Federal State Budgetary Institution of Culture State Central Museum of Contemporary History of Russia, a federal museum under the Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation. It is funded from the federal budget as a state budgetary institution. It was the Museum of the Revolution of the USSR until 1998.
after: A federal state budgetary institution under Russia's Ministry of Culture, funded from the federal budget. It was the Museum of the Revolution of the USSR until 1998.

before: Housed in the former English Club mansion at Tverskaya 21; the 2022 exhibition NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty drew almost 20,000 visitors in under two months with free entry.
after: In the former English Club mansion at Tverskaya 21; the 2022 exhibition NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty drew almost 20,000 visitors in under two months.

before: The State Stalin Museum is a Georgian state museum funded and protected by the Ministry of Culture and Monuments of Georgia and listed as a cultural heritage monument. Its restoration tenders run through the State Procurement Agency. Director Lia Okroperidze heads the museum.
after: A Georgian state museum, funded by the Ministry of Culture and Monuments and listed as a heritage monument; restoration tenders run through the State Procurement Agency. Lia Okroperidze is director.

before: The 1957 complex by architect Archil Kurdiani holds about 40,000 items; Gori's tourist centre counted roughly 162,000 visitors in 2018, and a room on repressions was added in 2010.
after: The 1957 complex by Archil Kurdiani holds about 40,000 items; Gori counted roughly 162,000 visitors in 2018. A room on repressions was added in 2010.

before: The museum is a state institution of the Republic of Serbia: the Government of Serbia appoints its director and the Ministry of Culture must consent to director competitions under the Law on Culture. It was founded in 1996 by the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by merging the Josip Broz Tito Memorial Centre and the Museum of the Revolution of Yugoslav Peoples. Entry is free.
after: A state institution of Serbia, whose government appoints its director with the Ministry of Culture's consent. Formed in 1996 from the Tito Memorial Centre and the Museum of the Revolution.

before: About 100,000 to 120,000 visitors a year, the most visited museum in Serbia; the complex includes the 1962 building by Mihailo Janković and the House of Flowers, Tito's tomb.
after: Serbia's most visited museum, with 100,000 to 120,000 visitors a year; the complex includes Mihailo Janković's 1962 building and the House of Flowers, Tito's tomb.

before: The museum is a state institution under Albania's Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation, which appoints its director. Its 2024 to 2028 reconstruction is funded from the state Public Investment programme (606 million lek) and the EU4Culture programme through UNOPS. It closed in March 2024 for four years of works.
after: A state institution under Albania's Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation. Its 2024 to 2028 reconstruction is funded by the state Public Investment programme (606 million lek) and EU4Culture.

before: The largest museum in Albania at 27,000 square metres, opened 28 October 1981 with the mosaic The Albanians on its facade; a Communist Terror pavilion was added in 2012.
after: Albania's largest museum, opened 28 October 1981; a Communist Terror pavilion was added in 2012 and it closed in March 2024 for four years.

before: The museum sits in the state Pancasila Sakti monument complex at Lubang Buaya and is jointly managed by the Indonesian Military (TNI) and the Education and Culture Ministry. It was built by the TNI History Centre, initiated by Brigadier General Nugroho Notosusanto and approved by President Suharto. Admission is 5,000 rupiah.
after: In the state Pancasila Sakti complex at Lubang Buaya, jointly managed by the Indonesian military (TNI) and the Education and Culture Ministry. Admission is 5,000 rupiah.

before: Opened by President Suharto on 1 October 1992 with 34 dioramas; it draws tens of thousands of visitors a year, mostly school groups, and a new wing opened in 2013.
after: Opened by President Suharto on 1 October 1992 with 34 dioramas; tens of thousands of visitors a year, mostly schools. A wing opened in 2013.

before: The 12 million dollar memorial was paid for mostly by Phnom Penh Municipal Hall, with the remainder donated by tycoon Ly Yong Phat, who also gave the land. The Win-Win Monument Construction Committee, headed by General Nem Sowath, runs the site and its museum. The Defence Ministry solicited public donations during construction.
after: The 12 million dollar memorial was paid mostly by Phnom Penh Municipal Hall, the rest by tycoon Ly Yong Phat, who gave the land. The Defence Ministry solicited public donations.

before: Inaugurated by Hun Sen on 29 December 2018 on an 8 hectare plaza in Chroy Changvar; the 33 metre monolith stands on a base with bas-reliefs, and the museum covers Hun Sen's achievements.
after: Inaugurated by Hun Sen on 29 December 2018 in Chroy Changvar; General Nem Sowath's construction committee runs the site and its museum.

before: The hall was established by a joint decision of the CCP Central Committee, the NPC Standing Committee, the State Council and the Central Military Commission on 8 October 1976. It is described by the Party as the highest memorial hall of the Party and state and a national patriotic education demonstration base. Entry is free.
after: Established on 8 October 1976 by joint decision of the CCP Central Committee, the NPC Standing Committee, the State Council and the Central Military Commission. Entry is free.

before: Opened 9 September 1977 in Tiananmen Square; it has received nearly 240 million visitors and over 190 foreign heads of state, with memorial rooms for Mao, Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi, Zhu De, Deng Xiaoping and Chen Yun.
after: Opened 9 September 1977 in Tiananmen Square; 240 million visitors, among them over 190 heads of state. Memorial rooms for Mao and five other leaders.

before: The museum is owned and run by the Hong Kong Government's Leisure and Cultural Services Department. The HKSAR Government describes it as one of its important cultivation bases for promoting patriotism. Admission to its thematic exhibitions is free.
after: Owned and run by the Hong Kong Government's Leisure and Cultural Services Department. Admission to its thematic exhibitions is free.

before: Housed in the 1887 British Lei Yue Mun Fort, opened in 2000 as the Museum of Coastal Defence and renamed on 3 September 2024 by Chief Executive John Lee; its permanent exhibition has 11 galleries.
after: In the 1887 British Lei Yue Mun Fort; opened in 2000 as the Museum of Coastal Defence and renamed on 3 September 2024.

before: The museum is owned by the Spanish General State Administration and is one of the national museums attached to the Ministry of Culture. Its directing bodies have depended on the Ministry of Education and later Culture since its creation. Contact runs through the cultura.gob.es domain.
after: Owned by the Spanish General State Administration, one of the national museums attached to the Ministry of Culture, under the education and later culture ministries since its creation.

before: Created by decree on 19 April 1941, shown provisionally in the National Archaeological Museum from 1944; its Ciudad Universitaria building was partly inaugurated on 12 October 1965 and fully reopened in 1994.
after: Created by decree in April 1941, shown in the Archaeological Museum from 1944; its Ciudad Universitaria building part-opened in 1965 and fully in 1994.

before: Fondazione La Quadriennale di Roma is funded by its partners: the Ministry of Culture, Roma Capitale's Department of Culture, the Lazio Region and the Rome Chamber of Commerce. It is based at Villa Carpegna, which also houses the ARBIQ archive of Italian contemporary art. The Lazio Region lists it among its grandi fondazioni.
after: Fondazione La Quadriennale di Roma is funded by its partners: the Ministry of Culture, Roma Capitale's Department of Culture, the Lazio Region and the Rome Chamber of Commerce.

before: Founded by resolution of the Governorate of Rome in 1927 and first held in 1931 at the Palazzo delle Esposizioni; it became an autonomous body by royal decree in 1937.
after: Founded by Rome's Governorate in 1927, first held in 1931 at the Palazzo delle Esposizioni, an autonomous body since 1937; based at Villa Carpegna.

before: Since 1 June 2024 the memorial is the property of the Czech Ministry of Defence, administered by the Military History Institute Prague. From 2000 to 2024 it was administered by the National Museum, which renovated it and ran the exhibitions Laboratory of Power and Crossroads of Czech and Czechoslovak Statehood. State ceremonies and military parades are held there.
after: Property of the Czech Ministry of Defence since 1 June 2024, administered by the Military History Institute Prague. From 2000 to 2024 the National Museum ran and renovated it.

before: Built 1928 to 1938 by architect Jan Zázvorka to honour Czechoslovak legionaries, with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and Bohumil Kafka's equestrian statue of Jan Žižka; the former mausoleum is now closed to the public.
after: Built 1928 to 1938 by Jan Zázvorka for the Czechoslovak legionaries, with the Unknown Soldier's tomb; state ceremonies and military parades are held there.

before: The museum is a Portuguese state museum. In 2019 it operated under the Directorate-General for Cultural Heritage (DGPC) as a twin pole of the Museu Nacional de Etnologia, and in 2023 Decree-Law 79/2023 transferred DGPC's management of national museums to Museus e Monumentos de Portugal E.P.E., supervised by the ministers of finance and culture. Admission is 5 euros.
after: A Portuguese state museum, run with the Museu Nacional de Etnologia by the Directorate-General for Cultural Heritage until Decree-Law 79/2023 passed national museums to Museus e Monumentos de Portugal E.P.E.

before: Occupies the adapted popular life pavilion of the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition in Belém with 1948 murals; closed in 2003, it reopened at reduced scale in December 2016 after a citizens' campaign.
after: In the popular life pavilion of the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition in Belém; closed in 2003 and reopened in December 2016 after a citizens' campaign.

before: The museum is a People's Liberation Army institution: Beijing's official tourism portal lists it as a deputy corps-level unit subordinate to the General Political Department, with the department's propaganda bureau as its professional supervisor. The Central Military Commission approved its name on 12 March 1959 and Mao Zedong wrote the inscription. Admission is free; the state rebuilt it between 2012 and 2017.
after: A People's Liberation Army institution, a deputy corps-level unit under the General Political Department, whose propaganda bureau supervises it. Admission is free; the state rebuilt it from 2012 to 2017.

before: One of the Ten Great Buildings for the PRC's tenth anniversary, opened 1 August 1960 at 9 Fuxing Road; after the 2017 rebuild it has 159,000 square metres, 43 halls and over 160,000 relics.
after: One of the Ten Great Buildings, opened 1 August 1960; since the 2017 rebuild, 159,000 square metres, 43 halls and over 160,000 relics.

before: The Shanghai Municipal Committee of the Communist Party rented the site from 1951, bought it in 1952 and has shown it free of charge since 1952. The state built the new 3,700 square metre memorial hall across the street at 76 Xingye Road, opened by Shanghai Party secretary Li Qiang on 3 June 2021. The hall is led by a Party committee secretary and director, Xue Feng.
after: The Shanghai Party committee bought the site in 1952 and shows it free. The state built the hall across the street, opened by Party secretary Li Qiang in June 2021.

before: The 2021 exhibition holds 1,168 items; the hall counted 12 million visits between June 2021 and 2025, with 3.23 million in 2025, China Daily reports. Xi Jinping led the Politburo Standing Committee there in October 2017 to renew the Party oath.
after: Xi Jinping took the Politburo Standing Committee there in October 2017 to renew the Party oath; China Daily counts 12 million visits since June 2021.

before: A state museum founded on 1 July 1950, among the first revolutionary memorial halls of the People's Republic; the National Cultural Heritage Administration rated it a national first-class museum in 2008. Admission has been free since the enlarged building opened in August 2009. China Daily describes it as one of three national bases for patriotic education, revolutionary tradition and Yan'an spirit education.
after: A state museum founded on 1 July 1950, rated a national first-class museum by the National Cultural Heritage Administration in 2008. Admission free since the building opened in August 2009.

before: The 29,853 square metre building at Wangjiaping holds over 38,000 relics and draws nearly 4 million visits a year; Xi Jinping took the new Politburo Standing Committee there on 27 October 2022.
after: The building holds over 38,000 relics and draws nearly 4 million visits a year; Xi Jinping took the Politburo Standing Committee there in October 2022.

before: A state memorial first built in 1958, moved to its present site in 1993, and closed in December 2014 after the central government approved its renovation and expansion in June 2014. It reopened on 19 September 2020 for the war's 70th anniversary with free admission. Xinhua describes it as a national patriotic education demonstration base; the museum's director is Liu Jingyuan.
after: A state memorial built in 1958 and moved to its site in 1993. Closed in December 2014 for a centrally approved expansion, it reopened in September 2020 with free admission.

before: The 182,000 square metre site at 7 Shanshang Street holds a 23,845 square metre exhibition hall, a 53 metre memorial tower, a panorama hall and a national defence education park; it recorded 12 million visits before the 2014 closure.
after: The 182,000 square metre site has a 53 metre tower and a national defence education park; 12 million visits before the 2014 closure.

before: The Bolivian state built the museum through the Fondo Nacional de Inversión Productiva y Social for almost 50 million bolivianos, opening it on 2 February 2017 in Evo Morales's birthplace. In June 2023 Culture Minister Sabina Orellana said the FPS and the Andamarca municipality still administer it because it was never legally transferred to the Ministry of Cultures, which pays only periodic security costs. The museum has been closed for over three years, Orellana said in December 2023.
after: Built by the Fondo Nacional de Inversión Productiva y Social (FPS) for nearly 50 million bolivianos. In 2023 the culture minister said the FPS and Andamarca municipality still administer it.

before: Three blocks totalling about 3,855 square metres on a 12,000 square metre site, with an open-air theatre and Andean temple, in a village of about 163 people; the Viceministry of Tourism reported 17,000 visitors in its first year.
after: Opened in 2017 in Evo Morales's birthplace, a village of about 163 people; 17,000 visitors in its first year, and closed since 2020.

before: The Politburo of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party decided on 16 December 1992 to build the museum, which opened on 13 December 2000 for Kaysone Phomvihane's 80th birth anniversary. It was built with non-refundable aid from the Vietnamese government, and in March 2014 Vietnam approved a further 14 billion dong (658,000 dollars) refurbishment implemented by the Ho Chi Minh Museum. The Lao state operates it as a memorial and educational institution.
after: Built with non-refundable Vietnamese aid on a 1992 Politburo decision and opened in December 2000; in 2014 Vietnam funded a 14 billion dong refurbishment. The Lao state runs it.

before: A bronze statue of Kaysone stands outside; the Party's Propaganda and Training Board stages its anniversary exhibitions here, opened by Party General Secretary Thongloun Sisoulith in 2025.
after: A bronze statue of Kaysone stands outside; the Party's Propaganda and Training Board stages its anniversary exhibitions, opened by General Secretary Thongloun Sisoulith in 2025.

before: The Bangabandhu Memorial Trust, founded and chaired by Sheikh Hasina, owned and ran the museum in Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's house at Dhanmondi 32 from its opening on 14 August 1994; Hasina chaired trust meetings there as prime minister. Banks donated 1,360 million taka to the trust in 2017 and Standard Bank 100 million taka in 2020. The museum was burned on 5 August 2024 and demolished on 5 to 6 February 2025; the Yunus government then revoked the trust's tax exemption.
after: The Bangabandhu Memorial Trust ran it from 1994; banks gave it 1,360 million taka in 2017 and Standard Bank 100 million in 2020. The Yunus government revoked its tax exemption.

before: The house where Mujib was killed in 1975, with a six-storey extension added in 2011; on National Mourning Day the president, prime minister and armed forces held state ceremonies there until 2023.
after: The house where Mujib was killed in 1975, with a six-storey extension from 2011; burned on 5 August 2024 and demolished in February 2025.

before: A state museum created by Ordinance 66-72 of 2 December 1972, inaugurated on 5 July 1982 beneath the Maqam Echahid martyrs' monument at Riadh El Feth, and placed under the Ministry of Mujahideen in 1993, which supervises it today. Entry costs 20 dinars and is free for mujahideen and soldiers. The museum's stated mission is to preserve the memory of the Revolution and the struggle against French colonisation.
after: A state museum created by Ordinance 66-72 of 1972, opened 5 July 1982 and under the Ministry of Mujahideen since 1993. Entry costs 20 dinars, free for mujahideen and soldiers.

before: Underground beneath the 1982 monument's esplanade, with wings on the resistance from 1830, the 1954 to 1962 war and independence; the monument was built by the Canadian firm Lavalin to a design by Bachir Yelles.
after: Beneath the Maqam Echahid esplanade, with wings on the 1830 resistance, the 1954 to 1962 war and independence; Lavalin built it to Bachir Yelles's design.

before: The museum operates under the Central Military Commission, the Ministry of National Defence and the General Department of Political Affairs of the Vietnam People's Army, the army newspaper Quan Doi Nhan Dan reports. The state funded the new 2,500 billion dong (101 million dollar) building on Thang Long Boulevard as a special-grade army project managed by the General Political Department; it opened on 1 November 2024 with free admission to the end of that year.
after: Run by the defence ministry and the army's General Department of Political Affairs under the Central Military Commission; the state funded the 2,500 billion dong building, opened in November 2024.

before: A 64,640 square metre building on a 74 hectare site with a 45 metre Victory Tower, over 150,000 artefacts and four national treasures; Party General Secretary To Lam visited on 3 December 2024.
after: A 64,640 square metre building on a 74 hectare site with a 45 metre Victory Tower and over 150,000 artefacts, four of them national treasures.

before: A branch of the state-run National Historical Museum of the Republic of Belarus, created by the Ministry of Culture and opened in 2012 for the 20th anniversary of Belarusian sovereignty, as the ministry's Svetlana Gavrilova announced. State bodies lent exhibits for its collection of over 4,000 items. It occupies the Presidential Administration building at 38 Karl Marx Street.
after: A branch of the state National Historical Museum of Belarus, created by the Ministry of Culture and opened in 2012. State bodies lent exhibits to its 4,000-item collection.

before: Six halls on Belarus from 1990 to the present, showing the first presidential decrees, state awards, gifts to Alexander Lukashenko and models of state buildings; Lukashenko called its opening of great political importance.
after: Six halls on Belarus since 1990, with the first presidential decrees, gifts to Alexander Lukashenko and models of state buildings, in the Presidential Administration building.

before: The AfricaMuseum is one of Belgium's ten federal scientific institutes and operates under the authority of the Secretary of State for Federal Science Policy, with the Belgian Federal Science Policy Office (BELSPO) commissioning its peer reviews. It employs some 190 people, including 50 scientists, and two thirds of its staff and budget go to scientific research. Director General Bart Ouvry heads the institution.
after: One of Belgium's ten federal scientific institutes, under the Secretary of State for Federal Science Policy. Two thirds of staff and budget go to research. Bart Ouvry is director general.

before: The palace is run by the Établissement public du Palais de la Porte Dorée, an établissement public à caractère administratif placed under the joint supervision of four ministries, those responsible for integration, culture, national education and research. The body was formed in 2012 by merging the Cité nationale de l'histoire de l'immigration, itself created by decree in 2004 and made an établissement public in 2006, with the Aquarium de la Porte Dorée. Constance Rivière is its director general.
after: Run by a public body under four ministries (integration, culture, education and research), formed in 2012 by merging the Cité nationale de l'histoire de l'immigration with the Aquarium.

before: The permanent immigration exhibition opened in October 2007 and was fully reinstalled on 17 June 2023 after a three year closure; the 1931 Art Deco palace by Albert Laprade and Léon Jaussely covers 17,000 square metres.
after: The immigration exhibition opened in October 2007 and was reinstalled in June 2023 after a three year closure, in Albert Laprade's 1931 Art Deco palace.

before: The museum is run by the foundation Stichting Nationaal Museum van Wereldculturen, operating since 2023 under the name Wereldmuseum, and has fallen under the Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science since the 2014 merger that created the National Museum of World Cultures. Its collection is part of the Dutch national collection. The lottery VriendenLoterij is a supporting partner.
after: Run by Stichting Nationaal Museum van Wereldculturen, named Wereldmuseum since 2023 and under the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science since the 2014 merger. VriendenLoterij is a supporting partner.

before: The museum had 317,572 visitors in 2022; it occupies the Colonial Institute building on Linnaeusstraat opened by Queen Wilhelmina in 1926, which it shared with the Royal Tropical Institute (KIT) until their separation in 2014.
after: In the Colonial Institute building, opened by Queen Wilhelmina in 1926 and shared with the Royal Tropical Institute (KIT) until 2014; 317,572 visitors in 2022.

before: The monument is managed by EGEAC (Empresa de Gestão de Equipamentos e Animação Cultural), the municipal company of the Câmara Municipal de Lisboa that runs the city's cultural venues, which took over its management in April 2003. EGEAC's 2025 plan and budget lists the Padrão among its venues with a forecast of 221,664 visitors. The Portuguese Republic holds title to the monument.
after: Managed since April 2003 by EGEAC, the Lisbon city company that runs the municipal cultural venues. The Portuguese Republic holds title to the monument.

before: The 56 metre concrete and stone slab on the Belém waterfront was remodelled in 1985 with an auditorium, exhibition halls and a rooftop viewpoint; EGEAC's 2025 programme centres on expansion, empire and colonial memories.
